title: Asteroids and dwarf planets
what: The Sun’s small bodies that are large or that matter: the main belt’s asteroids and Jupiter’s Trojans at least 100 km across, a few near-Earth asteroids, the centaurs among the giant planets, and the largest bodies beyond Neptune, where each was at the moment shown.
how: Not every known body, of which there are more than a million: the large ones, and a few that matter for other reasons. From the main belt, between Mars and Jupiter, every asteroid JPL’s Small-Body Database gives as 100 km across or more, some two hundred, from Ceres (939 km) down; and Jupiter’s Trojans of that size, seventeen, which share Jupiter’s orbit some 60° ahead of the planet or behind. Then a chosen few. Near the Earth: Eros and Ganymed, the two largest near-Earth asteroids, and Itokawa and Didymos, which spacecraft went to. Among the giant planets, the centaurs Chiron, Pholus, Chariklo and Bienor. Beyond Neptune: Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, Quaoar, Orcus and Varuna in the Kuiper belt, with little Arrokoth, which New Horizons flew past; Eris and Gonggong in the scattered disc; and Sedna, which never comes nearer the Sun than 76 times Earth’s distance. Five of all these the IAU names dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. It has named none since 2008, and many astronomers count others drawn here, such as Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna and Orcus: their cards say only what group each is in. Each body is a dot, the larger ones larger, not to scale: at the scale of the Solar System even Pluto would be far too small to see. Sizes are JPL’s where its database has one, as for the main belt, the Trojans, the near-Earth asteroids and the centaurs. For the bodies beyond Neptune it has none, so each is from the paper its card links: Pluto’s and Arrokoth’s from New Horizons’ pictures; Eris’s, Haumea’s, Makemake’s and Quaoar’s from watching a star pass behind them; Gonggong’s, Sedna’s, Orcus’s and Varuna’s from the heat they give off, which is less sure. Haumea is far from round (2,322 km long): its size here is that of a sphere of its volume, as Makemake’s is the shorter of the two widths measured and Arrokoth’s its length. Each orbit is a mean orbit fitted to JPL Horizons, as the moons’ are: the elements JPL publishes for a small body hold only at their epoch, and carried with Kepler’s laws alone they stray tens of degrees in a few centuries, as the planets pull on it. Most are fitted from 1600 to 2500, the years Horizons gives. Of the main belt’s 210, half are then within a degree of JPL’s place along their orbits throughout, as Ceres and Vesta are (within half a degree), and 169 within two; those held in step with Jupiter (the Hildas, which go round three times to its two, and Thule, four to its three) are swung by it most, up to 12 degrees off. The Trojans, swung to and fro about their places beside Jupiter, are within one to five degrees. A body beyond Neptune is fitted about the Solar System’s centre of mass (the Sun’s pull with its planets’ added, from JPL’s DE440), where its orbit is steady: about the Sun itself, which Jupiter swings to and fro, Sedna’s fit strayed 10 degrees. Drawn about the Sun, never more than a hundredth of Earth’s distance from that centre, all of them are within an eighth of a degree of JPL’s place. The centaurs and the near-Earth asteroids pass close to planets, and each pass turns their orbits, so no steady orbit holds them for nine centuries: Chiron’s would be 40 degrees off. They are fitted to fewer years (the centaurs from 1800 to 2100, the near-Earth asteroids but Eros from 1900 to 2100) and are within some two degrees there, Itokawa a little over three. Each card says how close its own fit came, and to which years. Outside its years a body’s orbit is carried on at the same rates: where it is along its orbit is then only roughly known. Left out for now: Apophis, Bennu and Ryugu, which pass so close to Earth that a steady orbit is tens of degrees off within a century, and the comets, whose orbits change at each return.
